sub-apps: **Scene** (the game-AI authoring scene, `/scene`), **Machinery**

`/machinery` render an arriving page that names the sub-app and the order
that lands it; the grouping convention for sub-apps is written once for people
and once for sessions; and the root still redirects to `/board`.

orders.title: WO-014 — The toolbox catalog as the app's own data: the `Tool` schema with five faces and the closed transform enum, the run's 3,463 map rows typed into tools by a checkpointed fan-out of at most twelve workers, the catalog library that loads them, the allow-list and scrub check that keeps intake out of the commit, and the catalog browser under the Tools sub-app

A and B, Enterprise Integration Patterns, Patterns of Enterprise Application
Architecture, RxJS core, RxJS practice, GEB map parts 1 and 2, Team Topologies

orders.title: WO-015 — The soldier scene: twenty units on a 2D canvas behind a renderer seam, a toolbox rail fed by the catalog, real-time-strategy selection, flock, arrive and a two-level formation with slot roles, a deterministic seeded clock, before-and-after trials, and the pure scene engine every later scene reuses
orders.objective:
at `/scene` the operator sees twenty units idling on a plain
field, each labelled with a lifecycle role; selects units as in a real-time
strategy game (click, shift-click, marquee, double-click for a squad, Escape
to clear, and the keyboard through the text layer); picks a tool from a rail
fed by the catalog (the first scene's movement and formation tools, the
typed rows the decisions file names by id at activation, about ten in design
B's first slice, plus the catalog's first three tools for each work the
summary lists, untyped ones shown as a special case with a clarify
affordance); reads its five faces and parameters
and sees the computed effect as ghost arrows before applying; applies flock,
arrive and a wedge, line or column formation with slot roles assigned from a
cost table; watches cohesion radius, collisions, heading variance, time to
objective and stalled units change in real time; compares the branch before
and after an equip with the first divergence marked; saves compositions that
survive a reload; and nothing leaves the browser. The same seed and the same
steps reproduce the same frames; under reduced motion the field is still
until Step or Play; the canvas is a projection of a frame the text layer also
renders, and the renderer sits behind one interface so a 3D painter can
replace it later without touching the engine.

switchable to WO-226) as a strip of beats left to right in recorded time,
the distance between beats proportional to the minutes between rows; above

operator as a figure at the edge; stepping the anchor fills a slot with the
agent that made the next row, labelled by harness, model and effort, with a

orders.title: WO-008 — Authentication and permissions for DotLn-Angular, legitimate from the Angular side: `auth` with an OpenID Connect authorization-code-with-PKCE client behind a port, in-memory token handling with single-flight refresh, expiry and invalid-token paths, the auth and permission stores, route and feature permission checks from a declared adjacency list, the mocked identity provider through MSW, and the failure-case matrix in unit and e2e tests
orders.objective:
a visitor to `apps/dotln` signs in through an OpenID Connect
authorization-code flow with PKCE against a mocked provider, holds tokens only
in memory, is refreshed once when a request meets an expired token and
signed out when refresh fails or a token is invalid, sees only the routes and
features the declared permission model grants, and every failure case in the
matrix below has a passing test; swapping the mocked provider for a real one
changes configuration and nothing in the Angular code.
orders.cost:

handlers (whose development signing key pair is generated when the mock
starts and is never committed), the `authHttpEvents` and
`sessionEvents` groups, guards, the permission directive, the `/login`,
`/denied` and `/account` routes, about 60 source files; adds one OpenID
Connect client library to `dependencies` and `jose` (development signing in
the mock) to `devDependencies`.
Removes nothing. Wall-clock: about 8 to 12 hours of executor work plus the
fixed cycle; unknown until run. Context bytes: WS-001 house rule 17, the
events and state documents, the client library's documentation, this order,
about 160 KB. Commands added in the target: none. Tokens: unknown until run.
Steps: 15. Re-mints: none. Refutations paid: nine receipts (001 to 009) name
this order, the last two judging the amended text.

criteria.text:
`grep -rlE "localStorage|sessionStorage" libs/shared/auth/src --include='*.ts' | grep -v spec`
   prints nothing, and the same grep over the files under `apps/dotln/src`
   this order adds or changes
   (`git diff --name-only $(git merge-base HEAD origin/main)..HEAD -- apps/dotln/src`)
   prints nothing; `grep -rc "console.log" libs/shared/auth/src --include='*.ts' | grep -v ":0"`
   prints nothing; and an e2e step after the sign-in reads every key of
   `localStorage` and `sessionStorage` and asserts that no value matches the
   JWT shape (three dot-separated base64url segments) and that no value
   equals or contains any token the mocked provider issued in that session
   (the handlers keep the tokens they issued behind a test-only knob the e2e
   reads), which covers opaque refresh tokens and the client library's own
   stores as well as house code.

`libs/shared/auth/src/lib/session/transitions.ts` declares the transition
   table for the six states and `transitions.spec.ts` asserts every state and
   event pair (the spec iterates the table and the event list, so an
   unhandled pair fails); `npx nx test auth` exits 0.

Unit specs exist and pass for each matrix row: timeout on exchange,
   `invalid_grant`, expired-then-refresh-then-replay, refresh failure to
   sign-out, invalid signature, wrong audience, skew within and beyond
   tolerance, two concurrent `401`s producing one refresh request (asserted
   through the MSW handler's call count), `state` mismatch, redirect loop
   stop, cross-tab sign-out.

`core` exports `routePermissions` covering every `BasePaths` member
   (a spec asserts the record's keys equal the enum's values and that
   `Board`, `Scene`, `Machinery` and `Tools` map to an empty list), guards
   use it, the `board`, `scene`, `machinery` and `catalog` e2e specs run
   unchanged without a session, and `npx nx e2e dotln-e2e` includes: sign in
   through the mocked provider and land on `returnTo` at `/account`;
   `/account` as the `denied` user redirecting to `/denied`; an
   element hidden by `*dotlnHasPermission` for a user without the permission;
   token expiry during use followed by a transparent refresh; refresh failure
   returning to `/login`.

The production build contains no mock provider code:
   `npx nx build dotln --configuration=production` exits 0, and for the
   development signing key's identifier (the `kid` constant) and for every
   path the mocked provider's constants file declares (both listed in the
   evidence README), `grep -rl "<value>" dist/apps/dotln/browser` prints
   nothing; the bearer token is attached only to requests under
   `apiBaseUrl` (a spec asserts a request to another origin carries no
   `Authorization` header); `jose` is listed under `devDependencies` and not
   under `dependencies` (the step 2 check prints nothing); and with `auth` at
   `null` the four public routes' guards admit an anonymous visitor and the
   login page renders the unavailable state (two specs assert it).

`docs/dev-reference/security/authentication.md` states the storage rule,
   the refresh rule, the matrix, the provider swap and that the server
   enforces authorization while client checks shape presentation only
   (`grep -c "server enforces authorization" docs/dev-reference/security/authentication.md`
   is at least 1), and `docs/ai-reference/auth-rules.md` exists.

sixteen beats as glyphs, a recorded lane carrying the operator's eight beats
as reference marks, and a twin lane carrying where the chosen variant of the
twin's patience stream fires after each hand-back when the order is replayed

have cost under the twin: the virtual close time, the twin's total waiting

agreement figure against it is computed or shown; WO-226 is the second order.

goalReview.goalStandard:
## Goal-aligned decisions

The [sequence](../planning/sequence.md) and selected work order determine
current placement and authority. The mission is the outcome; the critical path
is the dependency route to the next outcome. Useful prerequisite or
risk-reduction work must name the blocked outcome it enables. Process activity,
receipt volume and agent utilization are not progress by themselves. Goal
alignment grants no authority to reorder or expand work. In all phases, the Goal
Alignment and Process Cost procedure lives in the generated role skills
[WO-043, 2026-09-11].

Accuracy takes priority over agreement in every phase. The already-equipped
Correctness over Sycophancy rule applies to operator suggestions and the agent's
own premises equally: challenge unsupported claims, distinguish observation
from inference, state material uncertainty, and correct mistakes when evidence
changes. A confident request or an earlier decision is not proof of correctness.
Record material disagreement and its evidence in the same decision or phase
receipt; do not manufacture dissent or seek approval for ordinary judgment.

| Lens                                  | Decision question                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Policy resistance / fixes that fail   | Will local goals or guards undo one another?                                                              |
| Tragedy of the commons                | Does the solution consume shared compute, context or operator attention without accounting for the total? |
| Drift to low performance              | Does it improve an explicit outcome standard rather than normalize a worse baseline?                      |
| Escalation                            | Will additional process provoke more process or workarounds?                                              |
| Success to the successful             | Are credible alternatives excluded merely because the current mechanism already has investment?           |
| Shifting the burden to the intervenor | Does the solution remove recurring operator rescue or depend on it?                                       |
| Rule beating                          | Can the evidence pass without the intended behavior occurring?                                            |
| Seeking the wrong goal                | Does it advance operator flow and the selected product outcome rather than a proxy?                       |

Naive Interventionism adds the existing system's useful functions, affected
consumers, second-order harm, reversibility and smallest useful probe. NoOp
records what happens if nothing changes, why action or inaction wins, and the
evidence that would reopen the choice. Scale detail to consequence: explain
applicable risks and briefly group immaterial lenses with a reason; do not
manufacture eight repetitive paragraphs for routine edits.

Record evidence of benefit and the risks of intervening in existing behavior;
verification and handoff compare observed outcomes with the promised benefit.
Required legal or release actions retain their existing authority; NoOp is a
considered alternative, not an ambient veto or permission to abandon authorized
work.



Material choices and rationales go in existing phase evidence: per-order
`docs/evidence/WO-NNN/decisions.md` and cited product sections for work-order
decisions; planning dispositions/candidate records for planning choices; the
independent report or refutation receipt for its judgment; retained closeout
evidence for release decisions. The decisions index exposes per-order records.
Reuse and link a current rationale until its assumptions change; do not create
a parallel decision log or an extra approval ritual.


This launchpad is the operator's own DotLn instance. Its purpose is to plan and
run bounded, evidence-gated work orders across the operator's repositories, so
that every change arrives as a pull request the operator reads before it merges,
while the kit itself stays upstream and reaches this fork only through starter
updates. The first workstream is DotLn-Angular, an Nx and Angular monorepo that
serves two outcomes at once: the operator's reference Angular workspace, which a
colleague should recognize as the way the operator builds Angular, and the
operator's sandbox app, one app with sub-apps behind a menu: a scene for
authoring game AI from a toolbox mined from the works the operator reads, a
view of DotLn's machinery where a change to an agent's mechanisms shows what
changes in an example use case, the operator's own digital twin, and side
utilities. Every new idea lives there first as a toy the operator plays with
before promoting the ones that work, for the five UIFA roles, people and
software actors alike. The app is not wired to DotLn core: its data comes from
public mining into its own store, served to the UI through its own API, and it
informs the platform through GitHub issues, never by writing a control record,
so that the app improves the platform, the platform the starter, the starter
this fork, and the fork the app in turn. The critical path runs from registering
that repository in this launchpad, through one witnessed target order that
scaffolds the workspace, to a foundation where a feature is added by convention:
shared libraries, the component taxonomy, events and stores, the sub-app shell,
and a legitimate client-side authentication and permission model. Later
workstreams join the same way: one registration and one planning pass each,
with the fork's own machinery changes cut as self orders beside them.

episode.statement: Independent plan refuter (identity Entropy Reducer, mask Contra-Auguste, lens architecture-and-semantics) for one DotLn planning pass. Read exactly one input file, <tmp>/refute-prompt.txt (the canonical refute prompt: work order, compiled subject with the goal standard, sequence, cost table and five trap observations, and the six judged orders WO-014, WO-015, WO-016, WO-008, WO-017 and WO-018 in full; WO-013 carried by hash and not judged). Opened no other repository file. The host injected its session instructions and a git status summary into context; they were not used as evidence. Used only a local shell and Python to parse and print the prompt and to validate the output. Spawned no agents and ran no model tools. Made no repository or Git writes and committed nothing. For each order, answered the four acceptance questions: critical-path gate and NoOp cost in the records, the eight system traps applied to the order's own process cost, removal balance, and failure behavior. Wrote <tmp>/result.json (plan-goal-review-v1, checked against the prompt's closed schema): plan verdict aligned-with-findings; all six orders aligned-with-findings with 31 known-issue findings (WO-014 6, WO-015 2, WO-016 8, WO-008 5, WO-017 6, WO-018 4), each with a concrete reopening observation; no observed-failure findings, because every trap series shows worsening [] and reopenCandidate false and the judged rows carry null metrics; no hold reasons, because no observed failure exists and no vision passage id was supplied. Also wrote this statement to <tmp>/statement.txt.

orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: Gate: the vision passage names the sub-app shell as a foundation element, and WO-013 is that element. It unblocks WO-014 and WO-016, which declare hard dependencies on it, and through them WO-015, WO-017 and WO-018. It also settles WO-006-D005 (one app, sub-apps behind a menu). NoOp in the records: the cost-table row has metrics null. The observed gap is the NoOp state: one nav link, one BasePaths member, no sub-app. If nothing changes, every sub-app order has to invent its own route and menu placement. Action wins at a small cost (2 to 4 hours, about 24 files, no dependency). Its own hard dependency on WO-007 is not supported by its design (finding), so its place behind WO-007 is merge ordering, not a gate.
orders.systemTraps: Policy resistance: it respects the type:ui lint by keeping routerLink in app.ts and projecting the items into a template, so no guard is fought. Tragedy of the commons: the smallest order of the horizon. It adds one e2e spec (axe plus three viewport widths) and Storybook entries that every later gate reruns; otherwise immaterial. Drift to low performance: none. It adds a convention and keeps both the root redirect and the board route. Escalation: it adds two reference documents and a convention that every later sub-app order must follow and cite. Acceptable, because it replaces per-order invention. Success to the successful: a second app is rejected on the operator's recorded decision, and a router-owning menu is rejected on the lint axis. Credible. Shifting the burden: it assumes the operator accepts three group names, and there is no rescue path. Rule beating: criterion 6's grep for 'control record' passes on any sentence containing the phrase, including one that says the opposite. Low consequence, because review reads the file. Seeking the wrong goal: the three menu groups (Scene, Machinery, Tools) do not match the four sub-apps in the vision passage (scene, machinery view, digital twin, side utilities). The convention's 'sub-app' (a feature library) also differs from the objective's 'sub-app' (a menu group) (finding).
orders.removalBalance: No. It removes nothing: the board keeps its route and the bare link becomes the menu. It adds about 24 files, two libraries, two documents and a convention. Net additive by design; no process command is added.
orders.failureBehavior: Degrades. The root redirect and the board route are unchanged and asserted, so if scene or machinery fails to lazy-load, the old app is still reachable. The empty Tools group renders an empty-state line instead of a dead route. A navigation error reaches WO-007's error store through ErrorHandler. No refusal path is introduced.

findings.reason: The declared hard dependency on WO-007 cites 'the navigation store, the error surface and the persisted-state feature the shell and the arriving pages compose'. The design composes none of them: the menu template has no injection, the links stay routerLink in app.ts, and each arriving page has 'No facade, no store, no data'. The real coupling is file overlap, because WO-007 adds the notices container to libs/dotln/shell and app.ts. The stated reason is inaccurate, and it serializes a 2 to 4 hour order behind a 7 to 9 hour order even though the sequence format admits lane pairs.
findings.reopenWhen: WO-013's diff imports nothing from @dotln-angular/state, data-access or events, which would confirm the dependency is merge ordering only; or a later pass cites this dependency to block a lane pair.

findings.reason: 'Sub-app' names two different units. The objective calls the three menu groups sub-apps (Scene, Machinery, Tools), while the convention written into the two documents defines a sub-app as a feature library that exports routes. The vision passage lists four sub-apps: the scene, the machinery view, the operator's digital twin and side utilities. In this horizon the twin, a feature library with its own BasePaths member, is filed under the Machinery group (WO-017). The toolbox catalog and the toy shelf, which the vision ties to the scene, live under Tools, the side utilities. The convention documents will encode this ambiguity for every later sub-app to follow.
findings.reopenWhen: WO-017 adds /twin under the Machinery group and the operator asks for a twin group, or the 'how a sub-app is added' steps in sub-apps.md differ from the steps WO-014, WO-017 or WO-018 actually take.

orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: The compiled criticalPath field reads 'unavailable ... this instance has not declared a critical path', while the goal standard's own prose names the route: registration, one witnessed scaffold order, then a foundation where a feature is added by convention (shared libraries, the component taxonomy, events and stores, the sub-app shell, and a legitimate client-side authentication and permission model). This judgment uses that prose route. WO-014 is not itself a foundation item. It adds shared libraries (toolbox.ts in libs/shared/models, libs/shared/catalog) and a third sub-app (Tools) by WO-013's convention, and it advances the sandbox outcome 'a toolbox mined from the works the operator reads'. In the sequence it unblocks WO-015 (the rail is fed by the catalog and counted from catalog-summary.json), WO-018 (the catalog pipeline, catalog:check and catalog:report) and WO-008 (criterion 4 names BasePaths.Tools and runs the catalog e2e spec unchanged), so it sits on the dependency route to the auth gate. NoOp cost in the records: the cost-table row for WO-014 has metrics null and the compiled subject carries no NoOp record for it. By inference from the dependents' criteria, inaction leaves /tools absent and makes WO-015 criterion 4, WO-018 criteria 2 and 3 and WO-008 criterion 4 unsatisfiable as written. Tokens are 'unknown until run', so the saving from not running the workstream's largest fan-out is unknown, not zero.
orders.systemTraps: Policy resistance: the allow-list guard works by field name while every classifier reads the full map rows, definitions included; and TransformKind is closed and grows only by a recorded decision while `untyped` with any non-empty reason passes. The cheapest local path for a worker is therefore `untyped`, which the guard rewards and the objective does not want. Tragedy of the commons: up to twelve parallel workers each read 60 to 320 KB, tokens are unknown until run, and the order calls it the largest spend of the workstream so far. It is accounted per worker and the subagent count is recorded at handoff, but the total is not bounded in advance and takes twelve of the default subagent cap of twenty. Drift to low performance: no bound on the untyped share. Criterion 3 needs only three typed tools per work, so the catalog can pass with a weak typing baseline. Escalation: it adds two commands, a schema, three scripts and a rules file whose enum-growth rule adds a decision ritual for each new transform kind. Success to the successful: it classifies all 3,463 rows of the run's maps (existing investment) up front, while the horizon's consumers read tens of tools (WO-015's rail of about ten plus three per work, and WO-018's toys). Typing only what a consumer needs, as a smallest-useful-probe alternative, is not recorded as considered. Shifting the burden to the intervenor: the checkpointed fan-out reduces operator rescue, but criterion 5 rests on the workers' own statements, leaving the operator as the only check on quarantine reads. Rule beating: criterion 2 is field-name based, criterion 5 is self-attestation and criterion 4 passes with any reason string. Seeking the wrong goal: criterion 1 counts rows (3,463), a volume proxy. The outcome, a usable toolbox at /tools/catalog, is asserted only by e2e filtering. Observed: all five cost-table trap series (rule-beating, seeking-the-wrong-goal, shifting-the-burden-to-the-intervenor, drift-to-low-performance, policy-resistance) carry worsening [] and reopenCandidate false, and this order's cost-table row has metrics null, so no trap is observed failing for it; the lenses below are applied to the order's declared process cost and are constructible risks, not observed failures.
orders.removalBalance: No. The Cost line says 'Removes nothing' against about 40 source files, about 3,500 data rows, a schema, three scripts (merge, check, report), two target commands, the Tools home and browser, and two documents. As a product order the addition is the deliverable. The process share it adds (catalog:check, catalog:report, the allow-list check and the decision-gated enum rule) retires nothing.
orders.failureBehavior: Mostly degrades. A row the classifier cannot type becomes `untyped` with a reason instead of blocking (criterion 4). An unknown path renders the not-found page with a link back to /board (criterion 6). The fan-out is checkpointed, so a failed worker resumes rather than restarting. The allow-list check refuses by design (criterion 2), which is the correct failure for a clean-room guard. Unspecified: what the Tools page and WO-015's rail show when a lazy catalog chunk fails to load, and whether an incomplete fan-out leaves rows untyped or blocks the 3,463 total in criterion 1 (as written, it blocks).

findings.reason: The clean-room boundary is enforced by field name (definition, related, dotlnHooks, verified are refused; ids, short titles and generic terms are admitted), but nothing checks the content of the admitted strings. The classifier workers read the full map rows, definitions included, and write the five faces in free text, so a near-verbatim definition can land in a face or a title and pass both the check and the grep. WO-018 criterion 1 adds a --text zero-overlap check for its map; WO-014 has no equivalent overlap check of faces and titles against the run's definitions, and no criterion bounds title length.
findings.reopenWhen: An overlap check of every string in libs/shared/catalog/src/data against the run's map definitions finds a shared run of eight or more consecutive words, or a short title in the data exceeds the length the catalog rules call short.

findings.reason: Quarantine compliance rests on each worker's own one-line statement that no quarantine file was read. WO-018 criterion 4 already pairs each statement with the launchpad's read observation (the harness journal's row count for the quarantine path, or `unobserved`). WO-014, the larger fan-out over the same run, lacks that observation, so its evidence can pass without the intended behavior being observed.
findings.reopenWhen: The harness journal for the WO-014 session shows any read under the quarantine path, or the WO-014 evidence README lists a worker statement with no launchpad read observation beside it while WO-018's README carries one.

findings.reason: The objective classifies every row as one of four things (a tool a unit can be given, a scene element, a metric or a background concept), but criterion 4's status enum has three values (typed, untyped, background). No criterion asserts where 'scene element' and 'metric' are recorded. The share of `untyped` rows is unbounded, and any non-empty reason passes. Together with the decision-gated closed enum, the evidence can pass with most rows untyped and the four-way classification absent.
findings.reopenWhen: catalog:report shows more than half of the 3,463 rows untyped, or one reason string covers more than a tenth of the untyped rows, or the committed data has no field that distinguishes a tool from a scene element and a metric.

findings.reason: The goal standard says the app's data comes from public mining into its own store, served to the UI through its own API. WO-014 defers that store and API (candidate C1, a non-goal) and ships the catalog as bundled lazy data chunks loaded by libs/shared/catalog. No criterion asserts a data-access seam (a port or provider) that lets C1 replace the bundled source without edits in libs/features/tools or in the scene feature that consumes the catalog. The architecture document is the natural place to name it, and criterion 8 does not require it.
findings.reopenWhen: When C1 is planned, switching the catalog source requires edits in libs/features/tools or libs/features/scene rather than in one data-access provider, or catalog.md names no seam for the source.

findings.reason: Criterion 1 fixes the summary's invariant at a row total of 3,463 across eleven map files with their digests. WO-018 then adds Art of War, and WO-018 criterion 2 requires catalog:report to list `artofwar`. WO-015 criterion 4 counts the rail from the works catalog-summary.json lists. Neither WO-014 nor WO-018 says how the summary's provenance totals change when an in-repo map joins, so a spec pinned to 3,463 breaks, or the summary silently stops describing its sources.
findings.reopenWhen: WO-018's gate fails on a WO-014 assertion of 3,463 rows or eleven map files, or catalog-summary.json lists artofwar while its total and digest list still read 3,463 and eleven.

findings.reason: Tragedy of the commons and smallest useful probe: the order types all 3,463 rows in one fan-out whose token spend is unknown until run and is called the largest of the workstream, while the horizon's consumers reference tens of typed tools. The cost is recorded per worker after the fact, with no ceiling or stop rule declared before the spend.
findings.reopenWhen: The per-worker token record at handoff shows the fan-out spending more than the executor's own session, while WO-015's rail and WO-018's toys together reference fewer than fifty typed tools.

orders.failureBehavior: Degrades well; this is the best-specified failure path in the horizon. A persisted value that does not parse, or has an older shape, yields the idle twenty units (criterion 5). Under reduced motion the field stays still until Step or Play. The Null renderer runs the feature without a canvas (criterion 2). Unspecified: what the rail shows when the catalog chunk fails to load.

findings.reason: The rail lists the catalog's first three tools for each work catalog-summary.json lists (six works now, seven after WO-018), but the engine interprets only the first scene's movement and formation kinds, and criterion 1 makes the interpreter refuse every other kind as a no-op. As specified, most per-work rail entries can be equipped only to be refused, so the toolbox rail promises more than the scene does. No criterion counts how many listed tools act.

orders.failureBehavior: Mostly degrades. A failed sink post leaves the dropped idea applied and persisted (criterion 6). An unknown record type yields an `unknown` beat (criterion 2). A refused drop stays visible with its reason while the scene stays unchanged (criteria 2 and 7). The sink refuses to start on a directory that is not Git-ignored, a correct fail-closed guard. Unspecified: a persisted ideas value that does not parse or has an older shape. WO-015 criterion 5 specifies this case for /scene; this order does not.

findings.reason: The idea sink refuses a request from a non-loopback host, but a page on any origin open in the operator's browser reaches 127.0.0.1 from loopback, so a simple cross-origin POST (or a DNS-rebinding page) passes that test. Each such post appends up to 16 KB to the repository's intake, which planning passes read as raw material. The guard as specified does not cover the realistic sender, and the tests in criterion 5 cannot detect it.
findings.reopenWhen: A tooling test that posts from loopback with an Origin header other than the app's development origin, or a Host header other than 127.0.0.1 or localhost, sees the line appended rather than refused.

findings.reason: 'The repository's ignored intake' does not say which repository, and the sink accepts any Git-ignored directory. The goal standard says the app informs the platform through GitHub issues and never by writing a control record. A sink pointed at the launchpad's intake would be a file-system channel from the app into the platform's planning input that bypasses the issue route.
findings.reopenWhen: The sink's configured or default directory resolves outside the DotLn-Angular working tree, or the machinery rules file does not name the sink's destination.

findings.reason: The role-mechanism counts are asserted against 'the expected counts the executor set from the files read', so the spec agrees with whatever was read and cannot catch a misread. The parenthetical baseline is stamped at starter v0.96.1 (19 for the executor, 13 for each other role), while activation reads the starter the launchpad carries then, so a verifier comparing against 19 and 13 can fail a correct fixture or pass a wrong one.
findings.reopenWhen: An independent re-read of a named role file's Origin stamp at the recorded starter yields ids that differ from role-mechanisms.json, or the decisions file records a starter other than v0.96.1 with counts other than 19 and 13 and no reason.

findings.reason: The view's purpose is that a mechanism change 'shows what changes in an example use case'. Yet no criterion states how each of the six idea kinds (remove or add a gem or support, narrow knowledge, set the rung, add a wait, replace a prose section) alters the beats, and the fold 'decides nothing'. The e2e passes on a ghost, a presentation-only band and a caption even when every idea leaves the beats unchanged, which would make the redraw a proxy for the outcome.
findings.reopenWhen: machinery.md has no rule mapping each idea kind to its effect on the beats, or the e2e's applied idea leaves the beat positions identical to the before.

findings.reason: Persisted ideas and applied state survive a reload, but no spec covers a stored value that does not parse or has an older shape. WO-015 criterion 5 requires that spec for /scene, and its absence here means a schema change to ideas can break the shelf instead of degrading to an empty one.
findings.reopenWhen: /machinery fails to render, or throws, when dotln-angular.machinery holds a value that does not parse or one written by an earlier idea shape.

findings.reason: The objective labels each agent 'by harness, model and effort' and shows 'what it waited on', but criterion 1 limits the segment fixtures to ordinal, type, recordedAt, workOrderId, actor and verdict with additionalProperties false. Unless `actor` carries harness, model and effort, the labels have no declared source in the fixtures. Whether a model label is a configured pin or an observed value is also unstated.
findings.reopenWhen: The committed segment fixtures' actor values do not carry harness, model and effort, while the cards show them from another, undeclared source or omit them.

findings.reason: `grep -c '"recordedAt"'` counts matching lines, not rows. The check prints 16 only while the fixture keeps one recordedAt per line, so a compact or reformatted fixture holding sixteen rows fails it, and a line holding two rows passes it.
findings.reopenWhen: A formatter or fixture rewrite changes line layout and the grep count differs from the fold's sixteen beats.

findings.reason: The goal standard says the app's data comes from public mining into its own store. WO-016's data is scrubbed copies of the platform's WO-221 and WO-226 segments and the launchpad's own role files. This is provenance from the operator's own systems rather than public mining, and the order carries it with only a source.commit and an absolute-path check. Whether those sources are public is not stated.
findings.reopenWhen: The recorded source.commit for a segment, or the source file named for a role, is not reachable in a public repository.

orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: The compiled criticalPath field reads 'unavailable ... this instance has not declared a critical path', while the goal standard's own prose names the route: registration, one witnessed scaffold order, then a foundation where a feature is added by convention (shared libraries, the component taxonomy, events and stores, the sub-app shell, and a legitimate client-side authentication and permission model). This judgment uses that prose route. WO-008 is the only judged order that is a named critical-path item: 'a legitimate client-side authentication and permission model' completes the foundation the route ends on. The sequence places it fifth, after WO-014, WO-015 and WO-016. Criterion 4 couples it to them: Board, Scene, Machinery and Tools must map to an empty list, and the board, scene, machinery and catalog e2e specs must run unchanged, so the foundation gate now waits on WO-014's fan-out. It unblocks WO-017 (criterion 7 signs in through WO-008's mocked provider and needs routePermissions to cover BasePaths.Twin). NoOp cost in the records: row metrics null and no NoOp record compiled. The recorded spend is planning: 'nine receipts (001 to 009) name this order'. By inference, inaction leaves every existing sub-app as reachable as WO-008 itself leaves it (all four routes public), so the sandbox outcome loses little. The reference-workspace outcome and the foundation stay incomplete, and WO-017 criterion 7 cannot pass.
orders.systemTraps: Policy resistance: memory-only tokens conflict with the reload persistence other orders assert (WO-017 signs in and then reloads /twin); see finding 3. The routePermissions coverage spec forces every later BasePath to touch core, which is a convention and not a conflict. Tragedy of the commons: nine refutation receipts were paid before any execution, the heaviest planning spend on any order in the subject; execution adds about 160 KB of context and 8 to 12 hours. Drift to low performance: the failure matrix is an explicit standard. Escalation: repeated refutation and amendment cycles are the pattern the platform standard names ('the refutation pass must be made worth its cost before a later pass pays it again'), and this pass is the tenth payment. Success to the successful: an in-browser OIDC client is chosen and a backend-for-frontend is a non-goal, which fits 'legitimate from the Angular side' and stays reversible behind the port. Shifting the burden to the intervenor: none material; the mock's signing key is generated at start and never committed. Rule beating: criterion 1's storage probe reads only localStorage and sessionStorage, and the provider-swap claim in the objective has no criterion. Seeking the wrong goal: with all four sub-apps public, the model's runtime surface is /account (and later /twin), so the outcome served is the reference-workspace pattern, which the matrix tests honestly. Observed: all five cost-table trap series (rule-beating, seeking-the-wrong-goal, shifting-the-burden-to-the-intervenor, drift-to-low-performance, policy-resistance) carry worsening [] and reopenCandidate false, and this order's cost-table row has metrics null, so no trap is observed failing for it; the lenses below are applied to the order's declared process cost and are constructible risks, not observed failures.
orders.removalBalance: No. 'Removes nothing' against about 60 source files, one runtime dependency (an OpenID Connect client library, the only runtime dependency the horizon adds), jose as a devDependency, three routes, guards, a directive, two event groups and the mocked provider handlers.
orders.failureBehavior: Mixed, by design. With `auth` at null, the four public routes admit an anonymous visitor and the login page renders the unavailable state (criterion 5), which degrades to the pre-auth behavior. Token failures (refresh failure, invalid signature, wrong audience, skew beyond tolerance) sign the user out to /login. That is a refusal, but the correct one at a security boundary, and it is confined to protected routes. Redirect loops stop (criterion 3). Unspecified: a full page reload with memory-only tokens.

findings.reason: The critical-path foundation item is sequenced behind three outcome orders and coupled to them by criterion 4 (BasePaths.Tools, the catalog e2e spec). As a result, WO-014's fan-out, whose token spend is unknown until run, lies on the dependency route to the foundation. The coupling is consistent with the sequence, which this pass has no authority to reorder, but it means a stall in WO-014 also stalls the auth gate.

findings.reason: The token-at-rest probe reads every key of localStorage and sessionStorage only. A client library that persists tokens or refresh tokens in IndexedDB, Cache Storage or a non-HttpOnly cookie passes criterion 1 while breaking the objective's 'holds tokens only in memory'.
findings.reopenWhen: An e2e read of IndexedDB databases, Cache Storage and document.cookie after sign-in finds a value equal to or containing a token the mocked provider issued in that session.

findings.reason: Tokens are held only in memory, and the matrix has no row for a full page reload: silent re-authentication against the provider's session, or a return to /login. WO-017 criterion 7 signs in and then asserts 'the chosen variant present after a reload' on /twin. The two orders' semantics meet at an unspecified behavior.
findings.reopenWhen: WO-017's e2e reload step lands on /login instead of /twin, or WO-008's evidence lists no matrix row for a page reload.

findings.reopenWhen: The first real provider swap requires an edit under libs/shared/auth/src beyond configuration, or the authentication document states the swap without a test that runs a second provider configuration.

Unspecified: a persisted chosen-variant value that does not parse or names an unknown id, and reload behavior under WO-008's memory-only tokens.

findings.reason: WO-016's records fold already asserts the WO-221 operator beats and the seven gaps (87.8, 109.9, 1.7, 1.4, 2.1, 18.2, 5.9 minutes), and WO-017 adds a separate derivation script and order-221-derived-v0.json that assert the same figures. That makes two implementations of one fold. When the segment fixture or the readiness rule changes, the two can disagree, and neither order says which is canonical.
findings.reopenWhen: The derived fixture and the records fold disagree on any gap or on the waiting total, or a change to order-221.json updates one of them and not the other.

findings.reason: 'No interpreted model' is evidenced by the absence of JSON.parse in libs/shared/twin-model. Flips change a duration or multiplier live, so variants take parameters at runtime. A registry that walks a parameter or rule object, or uses new Function, satisfies the grep while the RxJS that runs is no longer the RxJS that describes the operator.
findings.reopenWhen: A variant file holds a step list or rule table that the registry walks instead of RxJS operators, or eval or new Function appears under libs/shared/twin-model/src.

findings.reopenWhen: A target-gate or CI run of twin:check fails on an absent base commit while variants.json lost no id.

findings.reason: Criterion 1 records 'the zero-overlap result of the check run with --text', but the order does not state the overlap unit: a word n-gram length, a character window or exact sentences. A check with a long window reports zero overlap for close paraphrases of the public text.

findings.reason: The toy-source tools for Meadows, Pirsig, Poincare, Gladwell, Taleb and the 5S set are 'typed into the catalog from public knowledge of the works', and several of those works are not public domain.
